rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to ensure all 10 compounds elute within the run and reveal the overall elution window. This gives a good first map of early vs late peaks and whether temperature or gradient compression is likely to matter.

All peaks eluted by 12.6 min and the estimated elution window is only about phi 0.09 to 0.38, so the first run wasted gradient range above the last peak. Narrowing phi1 while keeping tG and T fixed should make the gradient effectively shallower over the useful window and may improve the close cluster around peaks 5–7 without risking truncation.

Resolution is already perfect, so the clear opportunity is to cut time by steepening the gradient while keeping the broad window that eluted everything comfortably. This directly tests how much the critical mid-run cluster tolerates higher slope and may raise CRF if min resolution stays above 1.5.

The 10 min gradient is too steep and collapses the 5–7 cluster, while 20 min had ample resolution but unnecessary time. An intermediate tG should recover separation for the critical pair while keeping the run short enough to improve on the current best CRF.

The critical 6/7 pair is strongly slope-sensitive: too steep at 14 min, comfortably resolved at 20 min. Testing 16 min should be close to the shortest gradient that restores near-baseline resolution for that pair, with a good chance to improve the CRF further.

At 14 min only the 6/7 pair is limiting, and pairs with nearly equal slope often respond better to temperature than to more gradient time. A 5 °C drop should modestly increase retention and may alter selectivity enough to separate that pair while preserving the fast run.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by collapsing peaks 5/6, so test the opposite direction at the best fast gradient. A 5 °C increase may shift the crowded 5–7 region differently and improve the limiting pair without adding run time.

Temperature changes worsened the crowded region, so the cleanest path is back to slope optimization. Since 16 min is fully resolved but pays a small time penalty and 14 min is slightly under-resolved, 18 min checks whether the score model favors extra margin in resolution or confirms 16 min as the best practical setting.

The optimum appears to lie very near the resolution threshold between 14 and 16 min, and the CRF peak may actually sit at the shortest still-acceptable gradient. Testing 12 min brackets the slope response more tightly and checks whether the score can remain high despite lower resolution from the compressed 5–7 cluster.

At the best run, all compounds elute by about phi_e 0.55, so phi1 0.95 is probably broader than needed. Trimming the upper gradient limit while keeping tG fixed should make the useful part of the gradient shallower and may improve the 6/7 separation enough to beat the current best without adding time.

The upper gradient limit trim improved the critical 6/7 pair to just above the threshold, suggesting we can likely narrow the window a bit further. Testing phi1 0.80 keeps all peaks comfortably inside the gradient while making the effective slope shallower where the crowded cluster elutes.
Phi1 0.85 improved CRF, but 0.80 overshot and added too much time. Testing phi1 0.90 should locate the optimum upper gradient limit between the original broad window and the best trimmed window.

The current best is very close to ideal, but the limiting 6/7 pair is still just under baseline resolution. Adding a little gradient time at the now-better phi1 0.90 may push resolution to 1.5+ while still keeping the run short enough for a possible further CRF gain.

The best point remains at phi1 0.90, and the CRF seems to reward staying just below full resolution if the run is short enough. Testing tG 12 at this improved phi window checks whether a faster run can retain enough selectivity to surpass the current best.

The first peak still elutes well after the dead region, so raising phi0 may shave some early empty time without affecting the crowded mid-window too much. This tests whether trimming the lower end of the gradient can improve time while keeping the key 6/7 pair near the same selectivity.

Raising phi0 improved CRF substantially, and phi1 0.85 had previously outperformed 0.95 at phi0 0.05. Combining the better lower bound with a slightly narrower upper bound should further focus the gradient on the actual elution window and may nudge the score to the maximum.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so this is a confirmatory local probe around the optimum rather than a necessary improvement attempt. Increasing phi0 one more step tests whether early dead space can be trimmed further without sacrificing the now-safe 6/7 resolution.

Since phi0 0.15 still gives full score and the first peak remains retained, one more increase in phi0 efficiently maps the flat optimum region. This checks how far the lower bound can be pushed before the earliest peak becomes effectively unretained or resolution starts to erode.

We now know phi0 0.15 is still in the full-score region, so test whether a slightly narrower upper limit can shorten the useful window without losing the critical 6/7 resolution. This maps the 2D optimum around the current plateau while avoiding the overly aggressive phi0 0.20 setting.

Phi0 0.15 is on the full-score plateau, so the remaining useful local check is the other side of phi1. Testing phi1 0.90 completes the neighborhood around the current optimum and confirms whether 0.85 is truly centered in the best window.

We already have a maximum-score method, so the only remaining worthwhile exploration is whether an even faster run can also stay on the score ceiling. This tests a shorter gradient at one of the full-score windows to define the edge of the optimum plateau in tG.

We found a full-score plateau at tG 14, and a shorter run at phi0 0.10 lost too much resolution; phi0 0.15 may preserve the critical 6/7 spacing a bit better. This defines whether the best fast boundary depends on the lower-end trimming.

The optimum in phi-window and slope is established, so the last few injections can only test robustness around that best window. A small temperature increase at the proven full-score method checks whether a faster, hotter variant might remain on the score ceiling or confirms 40 C as the selectivity optimum.

The hotter variant badly hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so the final temperature check is the cooler side at the known optimal phi-window and slope. This confirms whether the full-score plateau is specific to 40 C or extends downward in temperature.

With the optimum plateau centered near phi0 0.10–0.15, phi1 0.85, and T 40 C, the only untested adjacent point is a slightly longer gradient at phi0 0.15. This final run checks whether that local variant also preserves full resolution and score, while confirming the robustness of the selected optimum neighborhood.
